tier_reason: The PLDI 2013 paper is peer reviewed, but every host carrying it (people.csail.mit.edu, commit.csail.mit.edu, courses.cs.washington.edu, web.eecs.umich.edu, dspace.mit.edu) is blocked here, so its numbers were seen only in WebSearch snippets; under the wave-14 rule snippet-only paper numbers stay tier C. The repository carries neither the expert baselines nor the paper harness.

corrections.claimed_speedup: PLDI 2013 abstract (search snippet only): Halide programs written in a few hours, with schedules found by stochastic search (autotuning), run up to 5x faster than hand-tuned C, intrinsics and CUDA implementations that experts optimized over weeks or months. Results-table fragments (snippet only; rows could not be matched to applications): '3.7x shorter / 2.1x faster' and '3x shorter / 5.9x faster', against baselines labelled Tuned C++, C++ OpenMP+IPP and hand-written CUDA on a quad-core x86 and a CUDA GPU. Pairing 2.1x with local Laplacian (262-line C++/OpenMP+IPP against 62 algorithm and 7 schedule lines, 335 ms vs 158 ms) and 5.9x with bilateral grid is the search agent's inference and is unconfirmed.
corrections.caveats: Numbers come only from WebSearch snippets of the PLDI 2013 paper (Ragan-Kelley et al.; the PDF hosts are blocked here, so the table was never opened); the snippet tool said the table text was garbled, so the row attributions (2.1x local Laplacian, 5.9x bilateral grid) are inferred, and the 5.9x row exceeds the abstract's 'up to 5x' without explanation. The baselines are the authors' 2012-13 expert implementations on 2012 hardware with CPU models, compilers and flags unconfirmed. The local Laplacian baseline calls Intel IPP library routines, so part of that comparison is Halide against a vendor library rather than against hand-written C++. The algorithm is the same mathematical pipeline on both sides, but the win comes from a different loop organization (fusion, tiling, recomputation, vectorization and parallelism chosen by the schedule and an autotuner), not from better code generation for the same loop nest. The repo does not carry the paper's baselines or harness; apps/blur/test.cpp does time naive C++, hand-written SSE intrinsics (blur_fast) and Halide side by side but publishes no numbers (enrichment lead). Halide is a C++-embedded DSL compiled through LLVM, so pipelines are callable directly from C++. License is MIT for the core; apps/bgu is Apache-2.0 (both OSI).

notes: Downgrade B to C: paper numbers seen only through search snippets and rows not attributable; the record's caveats already admitted this. Shortcomings: snippet-only paper numbers, 2012-era baselines with unknown flags and CPUs, IPP library calls in the local Laplacian baseline, win comes from schedule (loop organization plus autotuning) rather than codegen, no reproducible harness in the repo. Not a duplicate: Halide is not otherwise listed (halidecx/* entries in wave 10 are unrelated). Metadata checked: MIT, 6.6k stars, last commit 2026-10-09, active.

tier_reason: README Benchmarks table gives first-party ratios against SpecialFunctions.jl (Julia 1.7.2, Apple M1 under Rosetta) with no absolute times; the repo's benchmark/benchmark.jl times Bessels alone, so the comparison harness is not public. First-party with partial methodology is C.

corrections.caveats: First-party, run under Rosetta emulation, no compiler flags or CPU model beyond 'Apple M1', and speedups are ratios with no absolute times. The comparison harness is not in the repo: benchmark/benchmark.jl times only Bessels functions (no SpecialFunctions.jl calls), and its 'bessely' group actually times besselj0/besselj1. Most of the baseline is Fortran AMOS reached through SpecialFunctions' complex-argument path (besseli, besselk and non-integer besselj/bessely all call zbes* via openspecfun), and a Fortran-vs-Julia comparison is outside this catalogue's scope; only besselj0/bessely0 (2.5x, 2.3x) are measured against C code (openlibm j0/y0, which openlibm's Make.inc builds at -O3 by default), and that baseline goes through non-inlinable Julia ccall wrappers. Algorithm differs (Bessels' besselj0 cites the Cephes rational approximations, openlibm uses FreeBSD msun's), so this is a library win, not a language win. The Bessels.gamma row is a re-export of Gamma.jl per the README, not Bessels' own code.

notes: Numbers match the README table exactly; baseline description verified against SpecialFunctions.jl src/bessel.jl (openlibm j0/y0/j1/y1/jn/yn; AMOS zbesi/zbesj/zbesk/zbesy). Shortcomings: first-party ratios without absolute times, Rosetta emulation, comparison harness not public (benchmark.jl times Bessels only and mislabels the bessely group), mostly Fortran baseline, different algorithms, ccall overhead on the C rows. Metadata checked: MIT, 91 stars, last commit 2026-06-30, active.

tier_reason: README Benchmarks table (Apple M1 Max) is first-party; both programs are public (gpt2 driver, pt.py) and the current cmake/UserOverride.cmake gives gfortran Release flags, but the gfortran and PyTorch versions used are unstated and pt.py hard-codes OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, so the multi-core PyTorch rows cannot be reproduced from the repo as is. Not A, stays C.

corrections.baseline: HuggingFace transformers pipeline('text-generation', model='gpt2') on PyTorch, driven from Python by pt.py (transformers 4.26.1 per environment.yml; PyTorch version not pinned), with PyTorch's C++ ATen kernels and the same BLAS (Apple Accelerate or OpenBLAS); also picoGPT (NumPy)
corrections.claimed_speedup: README Benchmarks (Apple M1 Max, 20 tokens): with KV cache, fastGPT (Accelerate) 0.299 s vs PyTorch (Accelerate) 0.346 s (1.16x, derived from page data); fastGPT (Accelerate, fast_tanh) 0.288 s; OpenBLAS 1/2/4/8 cores fastGPT 0.837/0.514/0.341/0.339 s vs PyTorch 0.873/0.539/0.386/0.392 s. Without cache: Accelerate fastGPT 0.717 s vs PyTorch 0.787 s and picoGPT 0.765 s; OpenBLAS fastGPT 2.343/1.603/1.209/1.018 s vs PyTorch 2.356/1.520/1.104/0.997 s, so PyTorch is faster at 2, 4 and 8 cores. Total run including model load and Python imports: fastGPT (Accelerate, fast_tanh) 0.401 s vs picoGPT (8 cores) 3.445 s and PyTorch (OpenBLAS, 4 cores) 4.867 s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gfortran, version unstated (a gfortran=14.2.0 pin is commented out in environment.yml and postdates the 2023 numbers); current cmake/UserOverride.cmake Release flags: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -funroll-loops. PyTorch side: prebuilt binaries, version and build flags unstated.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers on one machine with one short prompt. The matmuls run through the same vendor BLAS in both programs, so the 3-16% gap is framework overhead (Python and HF transformers dispatch around each op, generate() bookkeeping) and kernel fusion, not Fortran code generation. The baseline is not a C/C++ program built at -O3: it is HF transformers on PyTorch driven from Python, timed by pt.py around the whole pipeline call (which also tokenizes and decodes), while fastGPT's 'Running model' time excludes its separately timed tokenizer. pt.py hard-codes OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, so the 2-8 core PyTorch rows needed an unrecorded edit. Flags are not equivalent: fastGPT uses -ffast-math (and an optional fast_tanh approximation) against prebuilt PyTorch. Without the KV cache, PyTorch beats fastGPT at 2, 4 and 8 OpenBLAS cores. The 0.401 s vs 4.867 s total-run comparison is dominated by Python imports and model loading. The README says speed comes 'by using Fortran' without a mechanism.
corrections.why_faster: Not Fortran code generation: both sides call the same BLAS for the matrix multiplies; fastGPT avoids Python and HF transformers per-op dispatch and generate() overhead, compiles its non-BLAS kernels (softmax, layer norm, GELU) with gfortran -O3 -march=native -ffast-math, and offers a fast_tanh approximation.

notes: Numbers match the README; record's '(1.16x, derived)' relabelled 'derived from page data', and the no-cache rows where PyTorch is faster (2-8 OpenBLAS cores) were added. Shortcomings: off-baseline (Python-driven HF transformers/PyTorch, not C/C++ at -O3), same BLAS on both sides so the gap is framework overhead, -ffast-math vs prebuilt PyTorch, pt.py hard-codes one thread, compiler and PyTorch versions unstated, PyTorch faster without cache at 2-8 cores, total-run row startup-dominated. Metadata checked: MIT, 199 stars, last commit 2026-02-14, active.
